Visible exit for Iran (deal on offer)

USA.name: United States
USA.notes: Constellations, chip design, AI labs, food/energy exporter. Reliability is the variable, not capability.

CAN.name: Canada
CAN.notes: First non-EU member of SAFE; uranium, hydro, nickel; AI talent sink. Latent via CANDU fuel cycle, no enrichment.

MEX.name: Mexico
MEX.notes: Labor and solar half of the North American continental system.

GBR.name: United Kingdom
GBR.notes: Storm Shadow, DragonFire, OneWeb (I on ISR/PNT since Galileo exit). Gravitating to EU on security.

FRA.name: France
FRA.notes: CSO recon sats, Ariane, SCALP; Alstom rail. Galileo shared -> I on PNT.

DEU.name: Germany
DEU.notes: Zeiss optics inside EUV (I, not S — tool is Dutch); Merck/BASF chemistry; SAR-Lupe; Siemens HVDC; Urenco share for latency.

ITA.name: Italy
ITA.notes: COSMO-SkyMed, Vega launcher; IMEC's European terminal candidate.

POL.name: Poland
POL.notes: Largest European land army build-up; SAFE's biggest borrower.

NLD.name: Netherlands
NLD.notes: ASML. The one hard technological line in the whole model. Urenco Almelo for latency.

SWE.name: Sweden
SWE.notes: Gripen, Saab; rail/HVDC via Hitachi Energy (ex-ABB) Ludvika.

UKR.name: Ukraine
UKR.notes: Most experienced drone/USV power on earth; sovereign on strike and USV, imports ISR/PNT. Refining mostly destroyed.

RUS.name: Russia
RUS.notes: War economy; refining down ~20% from Ukrainian strikes; every corridor in the model is designed to bypass it.

TUR.name: Turkey
TUR.notes: Baykar, ULAQ, Göktürk; Bosphorus; gateway for three corridors. NATO-shared weapons don't count as sovereign nukes.

AZE.name: Azerbaijan
AZE.notes: Zangezur corridor's eastern end; Turkish client, Israeli drone customer, Iranian irritant.

ARM.name: Armenia
ARM.notes: Syunik/Zangezur transit state; drifting from Russia toward EU.

KAZ.name: Kazakhstan
KAZ.notes: Middle Corridor spine; world's largest uranium producer; Baikonur leased to Russia.

IRN.name: Iran
IRN.notes: Three regimes in one (clerics, IRGC, technocrats). ~440 kg 60% HEU assessed at Isfahan. Succession unresolved; leader_born null until a consolidator emerges.

ISR.name: Israel
ISR.notes: Ofek, Iron Beam, Jericho, Dolphins. Intel Kiryat Gat is not leading-edge -> logic I. 20,000 km² with one airport.

SAU.name: Saudi Arabia

regime.source: V-Dem v15 RoW + estimate (MBS as effective ruler)

SAU.notes: $10-15/bbl lifting cost — last producer standing. Yanbu pipeline + Landbridge bypass Hormuz. Pakistan option on nukes.

ARE.name: United Arab Emirates
ARE.notes: Fujairah bypass; Etihad Rail; Barakah reactors (fuel imported, 123 agreement forbids enrichment).

QAT.name: Qatar
QAT.notes: LNG is the bridge fuel and all of it goes through Hormuz. Al Udeid. Turkey's alliance-grade partner.

EGY.name: Egypt
EGY.notes: Suez revenue; Gulf-Europe HVDC landing; largest Arab army.

IRQ.name: Iraq
IRQ.notes: Development Road (Faw-Turkey); PMF vs state; refining short of demand -> I.

SYR.name: Syria
SYR.notes: Turkish client, Gulf-funded rebuild, Israeli buffer in the south. Whoever controls Syria controls whether Iran's rail reaches the Mediterranean.

JOR.name: Jordan
JOR.notes: IMEC and Gulf-Israel HVDC both cross it; stability is the corridor.

CHN.name: China
CHN.notes: Sovereign on everything except leading-edge logic (7nm without EUV), EUV (none), and frontier AI compute (import/gray). Fertility ~1.0. No succession rules.

JPN.name: Japan
JPN.notes: Shin-Etsu, SUMCO, JSR, TOK, Tokyo Electron: the chemistry nobody can replicate. Rokkasho for latency. QZSS regional PNT. The hinge of the East Asian anchor.

KOR.name: South Korea
KOR.notes: Samsung/Hynix; Hyunmoo; Nuri launcher; shipbuilding at scale. Latency via technical capacity, no enrichment plant -> S is generous; keep and flag.

TWN.name: Taiwan
TWN.notes: TSMC. The contested middle of both systems; wanted intact by everyone.

PRK.name: North Korea
PRK.notes: Reference case for 'bombed-latent state gets the bomb'. Succession is dynastic — institutionalised in its own way.

IND.name: India
IND.notes: INSTC and IMEC both start here; Chabahar; the demographic counterweight to China in IFs.

PAK.name: Pakistan
PAK.notes: Saudi's nuclear option; Gwadar; mediator channel to Tehran.

IDN.name: Indonesia
IDN.notes: Nickel refining (Chinese-built); Malacca/Sunda/Lombok all Indonesian waters.

VNM.name: Vietnam
VNM.notes: Paracel claimant; China+1 manufacturing; the coast China's supply lines are hostage to.

PHL.name: Philippines
PHL.notes: Scarborough/Spratly front line; US EDCA bases; Luzon Strait.

SGP.name: Singapore
SGP.notes: Mature-node fabs, Micron NAND; the exception that proves the migrant rule.

MYS.name: Malaysia
MYS.notes: Advanced packaging (Penang) — the chem/packaging layer under TSMC; Spratly claimant.

AUS.name: Australia
AUS.notes: Indispensable and unconquerable, strangle-able: ~1 month fuel reserves, two refineries, undersea cables. Pine Gap. Latency = uranium + AUKUS reactors, no enrichment -> I.

NZL.name: New Zealand
NZL.notes: Rocket Lab Mahia -> sovereign launch geography. Refining closed 2022.

NGA.name: Nigeria
NGA.notes: High-cost rentier that craters first in the oil-decline scenario; Dangote refinery -> refining S.

ZAF.name: South Africa
ZAF.notes: Former weapons state; Cape route beneficiary if chokepoints close; Simandou-adjacent iron ore competitor to Pilbara is Guinea, not ZAF.

territories.name: Crimea
territories.notes: Annexed 2014. No plausible path back to Kyiv inside the model horizon except Russian state failure.

territories.name: Donetsk & Luhansk (Russian-held)
territories.notes: NE breakaway polygons are the 2014-22 'republics'; the 2026 line runs west of them. Sketch below carries the rest.

territories.name: Zaporizhzhia & Kherson (Russian-held, land bridge)
territories.notes: Includes the ZNPP. The land bridge to Crimea is the thing Moscow will not trade.

territories.name: Golan Heights
territories.notes: Annexed 1981; US-recognised 2019. Static in the model — a Syria treaty codifies it, it doesn't return it.

territories.name: Israeli buffer zone in southern Syria (post-Dec 2024)

geometry.geometry_source: sketch (UNDOF zone + IDF positions on Hermon and east of the line, approximate)

territories.notes: The 1974 disengagement zone Israel entered after Assad fell. A Syria–Israel treaty (hazard israel_syria_treaty) returns it to a demilitarised SYR/UN status.

territories.name: Turkish-controlled / Turkish-backed zone (Idlib, Afrin, Euphrates Shield, Peace Spring)

geometry.geometry_source: sketch (approximate; Turkish zones are now formally under Damascus with Turkish forces present)

territories.notes: Abu al-Duhur is here. Where Turkish AD arrives first and Israel strikes runways. Transitioning to 'Turkish garrison inside Syrian sovereignty'.

territories.name: Northeast Syria (SDF / integration zone)

geometry.geometry_source: sketch (approximate; March 2025 integration agreement partially implemented)

territories.notes: Controller nominally SYR after the SDF integration deal; contested because integration is incomplete and Turkey wants the YPG gone. Oil fields and the Euphrates crossings are here — the rail route to the Mediterranean runs through it.

territories.name: Gaza
territories.notes: Static in M1. Matters to the model through Saudi normalisation and IMEC, not through control change.

territories.name: West Bank
territories.notes: Static in M1.

territories.name: Shebaa Farms
territories.notes: Static.

territories.name: Kurdistan Region of Iraq

geometry.geometry_source: sketch (KRG-administered governorates, approximate; disputed territories excluded)

territories.notes: Autonomous under Baghdad. Turkey and Iran compete here; the Development Road skirts it. Static in M1, a hazard candidate in M2.

territories.name: Syunik / Zangezur corridor strip

geometry.geometry_source: sketch (Meghri district strip along the Araxes, approximate)

territories.notes: TRIPP (Aug 2025) makes it a US-managed transit route under Armenian sovereignty. Iran's red line is a change of controller, not a road. Control hazard is low but the stakes are the corridor.

territories.name: Nagorno-Karabakh (former)
territories.notes: Resolved by force Sept 2023; NE polygon is the pre-2023 breakaway. Kept for history rendering. Static.

territories.name: Abkhazia
territories.notes: Russian-garrisoned. Moves only on Russian state failure.

territories.name: Transnistria
territories.notes: Isolated since 2022; the first thing that flips if Russia fragments.

territories.name: Taiwan
territories.notes: The contested middle of both systems. Control hazard is conditioned on the taiwan_blockade hazard, not independent of it.

territories.name: Senkaku / Diaoyu (Nansei-shotō disputed subset)
territories.notes: NE polygon covers the whole Nansei chain; the dispute is the Senkakus only. Static in M1.

territories.name: Spratly Islands
territories.notes: Controller MIXED = feature-by-feature occupation. The naval-drone scenario makes every reef a Houthi.

territories.name: Korean DMZ
territories.notes: Static; the reference case for what a Ukraine armistice looks like.

territories.name: Dokdo / Takeshima
territories.notes: The irritant inside the Japan–Korea alliance the model needs to hold.

territories.name: Pakistan-administered Kashmir (AJK + Gilgit-Baltistan)
territories.notes: CPEC runs through Gilgit-Baltistan. Static in M1.

territories.name: Abu Musa & the Tunbs
territories.notes: Sit in the Hormuz approaches; IRGC Navy bases. Static unless Iran state-fails.

territories.name: Northern Cyprus
territories.notes: Turkey's EU/SAFE candidacy runs into this. Static in M1.

territories.name: Western Sahara
territories.notes: Static; included so the Africa map isn't wrong.

territories.name: Somaliland
territories.notes: Berbera — UAE/Ethiopian port on the Bab al-Mandab approaches. Static in M1.

territories.name: Alsace-Lorraine
territories.notes: The standing grievance in the FRA|DEU dyad the mid_force/mid_war templates are fitted across, and the reason the 1871–1914 peace between them is not evidence of contentment.

territories.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina (Ottoman → Austro-Hungarian)

history.source: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, Dec 1918

territories.notes: The territory that runs from the 1878 occupation through 1908 to Sarajevo: the chain the model should be able to see.

history.source: Cyprus Convention 4 Jun 1878 — leased to Britain against a Russian threat to Ottoman Asia
annexed on Ottoman entry into the war

territories.name: Tunisia (Ottoman regency → French protectorate)
territories.notes: Italy's grievance here is what buys the Triple Alliance in 1882 — a territory transfer that shows up as an alliance edge.

territories.name: Egypt under British occupation

history.source: nominal independence 28 Feb 1922 (EGY re-enters the actor set)

territories.notes: The corridor-driven intervention of the era: Britain occupies the state the Suez Canal transits, and stays 74 years.

territories.name: Heligoland
territories.notes: Traded for colonial claims and turned into the seaward anchor of the Kiel Canal position — a territory whose value is a corridor's.

history.source: Russian lease 27 Mar 1898 — the warm-water terminus of the Manchurian rail complex
lease Jul 1898, taken to balance the Russian and German leases

territories.name: Philippines (Spanish → American)
territories.notes: The acquisition that makes the USA a Pacific power and puts it on the CoW major-power list from 1898.

territories.name: Panama Canal Zone

history.source: Hay–Bunau-Varilla treaty 18 Nov 1903, after the US-backed secession from Colombia

territories.notes: A territory created to hold a corridor; the USA|COL mid_force of 1903 is the same event.

history.source: surrender Aug 1945; partition at the 38th parallel

territories.name: Libya and the Dodecanese (Ottoman → Italian)
territories.notes: The war that produces this is also the war that closes the Dardanelles in Apr 1912 — one Italian campaign, two corridor facts.

territories.name: Free City of Danzig and the Polish Corridor

history.source: Free City of Danzig under League of Nations protection 15 Nov 1920; Versailles gives Poland the corridor to the sea and customs rights in Danzig
Gdynia opens as the Polish bypass port — the build-around response to a contested transit right
1 Sep 1939: the demand for Danzig and an extraterritorial road across the corridor is the stated casus belli
Soviet capture Mar 1945; Potsdam confirms Aug 1945

territories.notes: A territorial corridor: the dispute is about transit, not about the land.

history.source: Allied occupation of the left bank from the Armistice, 11 Nov 1918
Allied evacuation completed 30 Jun 1930, five years early (Young Plan)
remilitarisation 7 Mar 1936 — the revisionist test the Versailles system does not answer

territories.name: Ruhr (Franco-Belgian occupation)

history.source: Franco-Belgian occupation 11 Jan 1923 to take reparations in kind: coal and the rail net
evacuation completed Aug 1925 after the Dawes Plan

territories.notes: Seizing a coalfield and its railways to collect a debt: the interwar's clearest case of infrastructure as a reparations instrument.

history.source: League of Nations administration from 10 Jan 1920; the mines to France for 15 years
plebiscite 13 Jan 1935 (90.7% for Germany); transfer 1 Mar 1935

territories.name: Memelland (Klaipeda)

history.source: Lithuanian seizure 10-15 Jan 1923; Klaipeda Convention 1924 makes it an autonomous region
Soviet capture Jan 1945; returned to the Lithuanian SSR

territories.notes: Lithuania's only deep-water port: the transfer costs it its sea corridor.

history.source: 12 Mar 1938; the actor AUT leaves system membership (data/history/actors.yaml)
Allied occupation from Apr 1945, four zones
Munich Agreement 30 Sep 1938; occupation 1-10 Oct 1938 — with it go the border fortifications and the Skoda works' rail approaches
occupation 15 Mar 1939; the first annexation of a non-German population, and the end of the Munich settlement

territories.name: Manchuria / Manchukuo

history.source: Mukden Incident 18 Sep 1931 — staged on the South Manchuria Railway; the Kwantung Army occupies Manchuria
Manchukuo proclaimed 1 Mar 1932; Japan leaves the League 27 Mar 1933 over the Lytton report

territories.notes: The territorial face of the two Manchurian railway records; the corridor event and the conquest carry the same date, 1931.72.

history.source: autonomous Republic of Hatay under French mandate, Sep 1938
ceded by France 23 Jun 1939 to buy Turkish neutrality — the Mediterranean terminus of the Iraqi pipeline region
Soviet invasion 17 Sep 1939 under the Molotov-Ribbentrop secret protocol
Soviet reconquest 1944; Curzon line confirmed at Yalta Feb 1945
retaken with the German invasion, Jul 1941 — the reason Romania joins
Moscow Peace 12 Mar 1940 ends the Winter War (war record: winter_war)
incorporation as Soviet republics 3-6 Aug 1940; the three actors leave system membership until 1991
Addis Ababa falls 5 May 1936; annexation 9 May 1936 (war record: italo_ethiopian) — the conquest the League does not reverse

corridors.name: Strait of Hormuz
corridors.notes: Effectively shut since Feb 2026 (tanker war). Reopening is a hazard; the transcript's modal path is a Hormuz-for-blockade swap.

corridors.name: Bab al-Mandab
corridors.notes: Houthi preview of the every-coast-is-a-Houthi world. Contested = insurance-priced, not closed.

corridors.name: Suez Canal
corridors.notes: Traffic halved by Bab al-Mandab; Egypt's fiscal stress reads this.

history.source: opened 17 Nov 1869; Suez Canal Co. Franco-Egyptian, Egypt an Ottoman khedivate
Britain buys the Khedive's 44% stake, Nov 1875 (Disraeli share purchase)
Tel el-Kebir 13 Sep 1882; British occupation of Egypt — the corridor-driven intervention of the era
Convention of Constantinople 29 Oct 1888: free passage in war and peace
Entente Cordiale 8 Apr 1904 ratifies the British position in Egypt
Ottoman/German raid on the canal 26 Jan - 4 Feb 1915; traffic suspended during the attack
raid repulsed at Romani 3-5 Aug 1916; the Sinai campaign pushes the front away from the canal
Egypt nominally independent 28 Feb 1922; imperial communications is one of the four reserved points, so the controller stays GBR
Anglo-Egyptian Treaty 26 Aug 1936: British forces confined to the Canal Zone for 20 years — the instrument Nasser abrogates in 1956
Italian entry 10 Jun 1940 closes the Mediterranean approach; Allied through-traffic reroutes via the Cape
Axis aerial mining of the canal and Suez roads, Jan-Jul 1941, closes it for extended periods (capacity is an estimate)
Tunis falls 13 May 1943; the Mediterranean route reopens and the mine threat lifts

corridors.name: Strait of Malacca
corridors.notes: China's Malacca dilemma. The rail corridors exist to make this number smaller.

corridors.name: Turkish Straits
corridors.notes: Montreux. Turkey is the gatekeeper of the Black Sea in every scenario.

history.source: London Straits Convention: closed to warships
Russo-Turkish war 1877-78; wartime restriction of the Straits
Treaty of San Stefano Mar 1878 / Berlin Jul 1878
Ottoman closure of the Dardanelles 18 Apr - 19 May 1912 during the Italo-Turkish war; Russian Black Sea grain exports collapse — the precedent Russia cites in 1914
First Balkan War; Bulgarian advance to the Chatalja lines
Ottoman entry into WW1 seals Russia's grain exit
Anglo-French naval attack on the Dardanelles 19 Feb - 18 Mar 1915; Gallipoli landings 25 Apr 1915 — the forcing attempt
Allied evacuation of Gallipoli 9 Jan 1916; the closure holds to 1918
Armistice of Mudros 30 Oct 1918; Allied occupation of the Straits
Treaty of Sevres 10 Aug 1920: the Straits internationalised under a Commission (never ratified)
Treaty of Lausanne 24 Jul 1923: Turkish sovereignty with demilitarised zones and an International Straits Commission chaired by Turkey; the Allied garrison leaves Constantinople 2 Oct 1923
Montreux Art. 19: the Straits are closed to belligerent warships — the closure that makes the Persian Corridor necessary

corridors.name: Taiwan Strait / Luzon Strait
corridors.notes: The blockade hazard closes this and the Taiwan control hazard reads it.

history.source: third Taiwan Strait crisis, missile tests

corridors.name: INSTC (India–Iran–Caspian–Russia)
corridors.notes: Rasht–Astara is the missing link. Bypasses Suez for India–Russia; the Russia terminus is why it's the corridor the allied bloc likes least.

corridors.name: Middle Corridor (China–Kazakhstan–Caspian–Caucasus–Turkey)
corridors.notes: Operating at low capacity; the Caspian ferry leg is the bottleneck. Bypasses Russia and Iran both.

corridors.name: China–Central Asia–Iran–Turkey rail
corridors.notes: The 'Iran paid to be boring' corridor. Its load_bearing_for CHN is the number that makes Beijing care whether Iran gets bombed.

corridors.name: Iran–Iraq–Syria–Mediterranean rail
corridors.notes: The land bridge Israel exists to prevent. Requires Syrian stability and an Iran nobody's bombing; both are hazards.

corridors.name: Iraq Development Road (Faw–Turkey)
corridors.notes: Bypasses Israel completely; Ankara is building it. The competitor to IMEC.

corridors.name: IMEC (India–Gulf–Jordan–Israel–Europe)
corridors.notes: Israel's only path to being on the map rather than around it. Gated on Saudi normalisation.

corridors.name: Gulf rail spine (Etihad Rail + Saudi Landbridge to Red Sea)
corridors.notes: Exports west without Hormuz. With Yanbu, this is why Hormuz denial hurts Iran and Qatar more than Saudi.

corridors.name: Zangezur / TRIPP corridor
corridors.notes: Links Turkey to the Caspian without Iran or Georgia. Iran's strategic nightmare; a bridge that 'collapses' is the covert option.

corridors.name: Gulf–Jordan–Egypt/Turkey–Europe HVDC
corridors.notes: The Gulf's next product is electrons. Same territorial-integrity incentive as rail, same transit states.

corridors.name: North American rail + HVDC spine
corridors.notes: The resurgent-US continental system. Gated on the US deciding it needs neighbours.

corridors.name: Panama Canal

history.source: Compagnie Universelle du Canal Interocéanique begins work Jan 1881
liquidation 4 Feb 1889 — the era's largest corridor failure (~22,000 dead, the Panama scandal)
US takes over May 1904 after the Hay–Bunau-Varilla treaty of 18 Nov 1903
Culebra/Cucaracha slides close the canal to traffic from Sep 1915 — the dataset's only corridor closure with no war attached
traffic resumes Apr 1916 (month is an estimate; the slides recur into 1920)

corridors.notes: The 1881–1889 French attempt is the model's only abandoned corridor: a corridor can fail without anyone fighting over it.

corridors.name: Kiel Canal (Kaiser-Wilhelm-Kanal)

history.source: widening complete 24 Jun 1914 — four days before Sarajevo; the fleet can move between the North Sea and the Baltic
closed to non-German shipping on mobilisation, Aug 1914
Versailles Art. 380, 28 Jun 1919: free and open to the vessels of all nations at peace with Germany — the interwar internationalisation experiment
Germany repudiates the international waterway clauses, Nov 1936
closed to belligerents on the outbreak of war

corridors.notes: The corridor fact most often cited as an input to German war timing in 1914. Recorded so the claim is datable, not asserted.

corridors.name: US transcontinental railroad
corridors.notes: Rail as state-making: the continental market and the army that closed the frontier ride on it.

corridors.name: Canadian Pacific Railway
corridors.notes: Built to hold British Columbia — the promise that bought the province into confederation.

corridors.name: Trans-Siberian Railway

history.source: Circum-Baikal line complete Sep 1904; single track — the capacity that decided the Russo-Japanese war
Amur line complete 1916, all-Russian route, double-tracked
Czechoslovak Legion seizes the line May 1918; the civil war is fought along it
Red Army retakes the line Oct 1920; capacity recovers slowly

corridors.notes: capacity is the through-traffic share the line can actually carry (estimate); the 1904 single track is the war variable.

corridors.name: Chinese Eastern Railway (Chita–Harbin–Vladivostok)

history.source: through service Jul 1903 — the shortcut that shortens the Trans-Siberian by 900 km
Treaty of Portsmouth 5 Sep 1905: Russia keeps the CER north of Changchun
Russian Revolution Nov 1917; the line falls to the CER Zone administration and the Allied/Czechoslovak intervention
Sino-Soviet agreement 31 May 1924: joint Chinese-Soviet management
Chinese seizure Jul 1929, Soviet offensive; Khabarovsk Protocol 22 Dec 1929 restores joint control — the war record cer_1929
USSR sells the CER to Manchukuo for 140m yen, 23 Mar 1935 — a corridor liquidated to avoid a war
Soviet seizure Aug 1945; merged into the Chinese Changchun Railway

corridors.notes: The densest dyad of the turn (CHN|RUS: 8 mid_force, 2 mid_war 1870–1914) is about this line and the lease at its end.

corridors.name: South Manchuria Railway (Harbin–Changchun–Port Arthur)

history.source: Russian Liaodong lease 27 Mar 1898; branch to Port Arthur begun
Treaty of Portsmouth 5 Sep 1905 transfers Changchun–Port Arthur to Japan
South Manchuria Railway Co. chartered Nov 1906 — a corridor operating as a colonial state
Twenty-One Demands, 25 May 1915: the Kwantung lease and the SMR extended to 99 years
Zhang Zuolin killed by a Kwantung Army bomb at the Huanggutun rail crossing, 4 Jun 1928
Liutiaohu demolition on the SMR track 18 Sep 1931 — the pretext for the Manchurian War (war record: manchurian)
Manchukuo proclaimed 1 Mar 1932; the SMR Co. becomes the state's spine

corridors.notes: A corridor changing hands as a war outcome: the clearest case in the dataset.

corridors.name: Berlin–Baghdad railway

history.source: Anatolian Railway concession, Deutsche Bank, Oct 1888
Anglo-German convention 15 Jun 1914: Britain accepts the line, Basra terminus, no Gulf extension — the corridor dispute is settled six weeks before the DEU|GBR war
through service 1940, after the empires that fought over it were gone

corridors.notes: The stated test for the corridor dampener: if a contested corridor raises dyadic tension, DEU|GBR hazard should rise 1903–1914 and fall after Jun 1914. The 1914.45 settlement six weeks before the war is evidence against the dampener as written in docs/schema.md — the test, not the conclusion.

corridors.name: Hejaz railway (Damascus–Medina)

history.source: construction begins Sep 1900, funded by subscription across the Muslim world
Arab Revolt sabotage 1916-18 — the first modern rail-cutting campaign
never restored north of Medina after the Arab Revolt; the mandate borders cut the line

corridors.notes: Pilgrimage cover for a troop-movement line; its destruction is the era's cleanest corridor-denial campaign.

corridors.name: Cape-to-Cairo railway

history.source: Rhodes's project; the northern and southern ends were built, the middle never was
estimate: no through line was ever built; the Benguela route (1931) took the traffic the middle section would have carried

corridors.notes: The counterfactual corridor — kept as a negative case for corridor_status: most planned corridors are never built.

history.source: Bulawayo reached Nov 1897 — the southern half of the Cape-to-Cairo project

corridors.name: Uganda railway (Mombasa–Kisumu)
corridors.notes: Built to reach the Nile headwaters — the corridor rationale for the British position in Uganda and, through it, Egypt.

corridors.name: Trans-Caspian railway (Krasnovodsk–Samarkand–Tashkent)
corridors.notes: The corridor behind the Panjdeh crisis and the Anglo-Russian Great Game: Russian troops within rail reach of Herat.

history.source: through service 1883 — the rail predecessor of the 1906 pipeline
completed 1906; the world's first long-distance product pipeline

corridors.name: Gotthard rail tunnel
corridors.notes: Alpine transit as neutrality's product: Swiss neutrality is load-bearing for its neighbours because of the tunnels.

corridors.name: Eastern Telegraph imperial cable spine

history.source: Japanese seizure of the Singapore-Hong Kong segments, Feb 1942

corridors.notes: The British cable monopoly is the ISR chokepoint of the era: almost every foreign ministry's traffic lands on British-owned cable at some point.

corridors.name: All-Red Pacific cable (Vancouver–Fanning–Fiji–Norfolk–Australia/NZ)

history.source: first message 31 Oct 1902 — routed to touch no foreign soil: the deliberate bypass
SMS Nurnberg cuts the cable at Fanning Island 7 Sep 1914 — the bypass built in 1902 to touch no foreign soil is cut anyway

corridors.notes: A corridor built to remove a dependency rather than to carry trade. The bypass response is what corridor_status should predict.

corridors.name: German transatlantic cables (Emden–Azores–New York)

history.source: cut by CS Alert in the Channel, 5 Aug 1914 — Germany's direct link to neutral opinion severed on day one

corridors.notes: Built as a bypass of the British spine and cut anyway: bypass reduces exposure only where the bypass avoids the adversary's water.

corridors.name: Spanish colonial cables (Cuba, Philippines)

history.source: US Navy cuts the Manila cable 2 May and the Cienfuegos cable 11 May 1898 — the first deliberate infrastructure denial of a war

corridors.notes: With spanish_american already in events.yaml, this and german_atlantic_cables are the two cleanest cut-the-cable observations in the dataset.

history.source: closed on the founding of Israel, 1948 — a corridor killed by a new border
transit disputes and the Lebanese civil war
opened 1964 — the corridor that made the Warsaw Pact an energy system
first oil at Ceyhan Jun 2006 — the first post-Soviet corridor that bypasses Russia and Iran

corridors.name: Ofotbanen / Malmbanan (Kiruna–Narvik iron-ore railway)
corridors.notes: Germany drew roughly 9-11 Mt/yr of Swedish iron ore, about 40% of consumption; the Gulf of Bothnia freezes, so the winter route is Narvik. The corridor is the stated object of both the Allied mining of the Norwegian Leads and the German invasion, 8-9 Apr 1940.

history.source: Allied mining of the Leads 8 Apr 1940 and the German invasion 9 Apr 1940; Narvik changes hands three times

corridors.name: Trans-Iranian Railway (the Persian Corridor)
corridors.notes: The era's cleanest instance of chokepoint closure creating a corridor: with the Turkish Straits shut to belligerents under Montreux Art. 19 and the Arctic route contested, roughly 4.16 Mt of Lend-Lease moved to the USSR through Iran. Built debt-free on sugar and tea duties, then taken by the states it was built to keep out.

history.source: through service Bandar Shahpur–Tehran–Bandar Shah, Aug 1938
Anglo-Soviet invasion 25-31 Aug 1941 (war record: iran_1941); joint British/Soviet operation of the line

corridors.name: Burma Road (Lashio–Kunming)
corridors.notes: China's last land supply route after the coast fell. The Jul-Oct 1940 closure is a corridor shut by diplomatic pressure with no war on any transit state — the second falsifier for chokepoint_status, whose covariates are all conflict terms.

history.source: Britain closes the Burmese section to Chinese war material 18 Jul 1940 under Japanese pressure
Japanese conquest of Burma, Apr-May 1942; substituted by the Hump airlift
Ledo/Stilwell Road through to Kunming, Jan 1945

corridors.name: Mediterranean through-route (Gibraltar–Sicilian Narrows–Suez)
corridors.notes: Without this record the Suez entry asserts an open canal for 1940-43, the years nobody could reach it: Allied traffic went round the Cape, adding roughly 40 days per voyage.

history.source: Entente Cordiale 8 Apr 1904; the route is British-Italian-French in peacetime
Italian entry 10 Jun 1940: Allied through-traffic reroutes via the Cape
first through convoy since 1940 sails in Aug 1943 (date is an estimate)
